`@supatype/client` talks to your project's REST, auth, storage, realtime and functions. Its types come from your schema, so a wrong table or column fails the build.

Pre-1.0: APIs and config may change between releases.

<h2 id="setup">Create the client</h2>

Import `createClient` from the client file the CLI generates, not from `@supatype/client` directly. The generated file tells the client which models keep drafts.

```ts title="src/supatype.ts"
import { createClient } from "../supatype/generated/client"

export const supatype = createClient({
  url: import.meta.env.VITE_SUPATYPE_URL,
  anonKey: import.meta.env.VITE_SUPATYPE_ANON_KEY,
})
```

Every page in these docs imports the client from this one file. `supatype init`, `supatype dev` and `supatype keys --write` write `VITE_SUPATYPE_URL` and `VITE_SUPATYPE_ANON_KEY` to `.env`, with `PUBLIC_` and `EXPO_PUBLIC_` copies for other frameworks. Read them rather than copying a URL from an example: `init` picks a free gateway port for each project, kept in `.env` as `API_EXTERNAL_URL`.

The session is saved and restored by default. Pass `auth: { persistSession: false }` to keep it in memory only.

`createClient` takes these options as well as `url` and `anonKey`:

| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `serviceRoleKey` | Bypasses row-level security. Use it only on a server or in a trusted tool, and never ship it to a browser. |
| `headers` | Headers sent with every request. Pass a function to have it read on each request. |
| `auth.storageKey` | Key the session is saved under. Default `"supatype.auth.session"`. |
| `auth.storage` | Your own session store with `getItem`, `setItem` and `removeItem`, such as AsyncStorage in React Native. |
| `auth.cookiePrefix` | Prefix of the auth cookie `@supatype/ssr` reads. Default `"st"`. |
| `timeout`, `retry` | See [Timeouts and retries](#timeouts-and-retries). |
| `initialSession` | A session to start with. `@supatype/ssr` uses it to hand a cookie session to the client. |
| `queryCache` | The in-memory cache for `.cache()` reads. Default: one shared cache. |

<h2 id="types">Generated types</h2>

`supatype dev`, `supatype push` and `supatype generate` write these files. Do not edit them.

| File | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `supatype/generated/client.ts` | The `createClient` to import, the table types, the columns that keep exact values and the models that keep drafts. It also re-exports `@supatype/client` |
| `supatype/generated/index.d.ts` | Row, insert and update types for each table |
| `types/database.ts` | The `Database` type, for code that wants the raw shapes |

Tables are named as in the database: `post`, `comment`, `post_tag`. Calling `createClient` with no type argument picks up the generated types. To type a client against a schema you do not generate, such as a second project or a test double, pass the database type: `createClient<MyDatabase>({ ... })`.

Exact numbers keep every digit when you import from the generated `client.ts`. A `BigInt` column reads as a `bigint`. `Decimal` and `Money` columns read as strings.

A number too large for JavaScript, in a column the client does not know, returns an error that names the column. This usually happens in an embed: select the column directly instead.

<h2 id="read">Read rows</h2>

```ts
const { data: posts, error } = await supatype
  .from("post")
  .select("id, title, slug, author(name), comment(body)")
  .order("published_at", { ascending: false })
  .limit(10)

if (error) throw new Error(error.message)
for (const post of posts ?? []) console.log(post.title, post.author?.name)
```

`select` takes a list of columns. The result type follows the list. `*` selects every column.

Name a related table to embed it: `author(name)` follows `author_id`, and `comment(body)` lists a post's comments. A many-to-many relation embeds through its junction table: `select("title, tag(name)")`.

A to-one embed can be `null`. Write `author!inner(name)` to keep only posts that have one. Rename an embed with `writer:author(name)`.

`single()` returns one row and errors when there is not exactly one. `maybeSingle()` returns `null` for no row.

```ts
const { data: post } = await supatype.from("post").select("*").eq("slug", "hello-world").maybeSingle()
console.log(post?.title)
```

`count` is `null` unless you ask for it:

```ts
const { count } = await supatype.from("post").select("id", { count: "exact" }).eq("kind", "news")
console.log(count)
```

<h2 id="filters">Filters</h2>

| Filter | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `eq`, `neq` | equal, not equal |
| `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte` | greater or less than |
| `like`, `ilike` | a pattern, `ilike` ignores case |
| `in` | any of a list |
| `is` | `null`, `true` or `false` |
| `contains`, `containedBy` | an array, range or jsonb column that holds the value, or is held by it |
| `not`, `or`, `match` | negation, either filter, several equalities |

```ts
await supatype.from("post").select("id").in("kind", ["news", "guide"]).is("published_at", null)
await supatype.from("post").select("id").ilike("title", "%hello%").range(0, 19)
```

Reads also take `order`, `limit` and `range`. Filters work on `update` and `delete` too.

<h2 id="write">Insert, update, delete</h2>

```ts
const { data: created, error: insertError } = await supatype
  .from("post")
  .insert({ title: "Draft idea", body: "Plain text is fine.", kind: "guide", author_id: userId })
  .select("id")
  .single()
if (insertError || !created) throw new Error(insertError?.message ?? "insert failed")

await supatype.from("comment").update({ body: "Edited" }).eq("id", commentId)
await supatype.from("comment").delete().eq("id", commentId)
```

A write returns no rows unless you add `.select()`. On a delete, `.select()` returns the rows it deleted. `upsert` inserts or updates by primary key.

A `RichText` field takes a plain string on write.

Some owner columns can be left out. A `SupatypeAuthUserId` field that the `create` rule names in `Owner<>`, and that has no default of its own, defaults to the caller. A relation's key, such as `author_id`, is not filled in, so send it.

<h2 id="drafts">Drafts and publishing</h2>

On a model with `versions: { drafts: true }`, `update` saves a draft. The live row does not change until the record is published.

```ts
// Save a draft
await supatype.from("post").update({ title: "Better title" }).eq("id", postId)

// Save and publish in one call
await supatype.from("post").update({ title: "Final title" }, { publish: true }).eq("id", postId)

// Read drafts
const { data: drafts } = await supatype.from("post").draft().select("id, title").eq("id", postId)

// Publish the saved draft
await supatype.rpc("publish", { model_table: "post", record_id: postId }, { schema: "supatype" })
```

`insert` on a drafts model creates a draft record. Publish it to make it live. A plain `select()` reads the live table, which holds the published values.

`{ publish: true }` is only accepted on drafts models, and only when the client comes from the generated file.

<h2 id="auth">Auth</h2>

```ts
await supatype.auth.signUp({ email: "alex@example.com", password: "a-long-password" })

const { data, error: signInError } = await supatype.auth.signInWithPassword({
  email: "alex@example.com",
  password: "a-long-password",
})
if (signInError) throw new Error(signInError.message)
console.log(data.session?.user.id)

const { data: { session } } = await supatype.auth.getSession()
console.log(session?.accessToken)

const { data: { subscription } } = supatype.auth.onAuthStateChange((event, current) => {
  console.log(event, current?.user.email)
})
subscription.unsubscribe()

await supatype.auth.signOut()
```

Once signed in, every request carries the user's token, so access rules see them. `onAuthStateChange` calls back at once with the current state, then on each change.

When the project asks new users to confirm their email, `signUp` returns `session: null` and does not sign the user in. They sign in once they have confirmed.

`getUser()` fetches the user from the server. Magic links, OAuth, one-time codes and MFA are on `supatype.auth` too.

<h2 id="storage">Storage</h2>

```ts
const bucket = supatype.storage.from("covers")

const { data: upload, error: uploadError } = await bucket.upload(`${userId}/cover.png`, file, {
  contentType: "image/png",
  upsert: true,
})
if (uploadError || !upload) throw new Error(uploadError?.message ?? "upload failed")

const { data: { publicUrl } } = bucket.getPublicUrl(upload.path)
const { data: signed } = await bucket.createSignedUrl(upload.path, 60)
console.log(publicUrl, signed?.signedUrl)
```

`getPublicUrl` works for public buckets. `createSignedUrl` gives a link that expires after the number of seconds you pass. `download`, `list` and `remove` are on the bucket too.

An `ImageAsset` or `FileAsset` column holds `{ bucket, path }`, not a URL. `publicUrl` builds the URL from it, and returns `null` for an empty column:

```ts
const { data: post } = await supatype.from("post").select("title, cover").eq("slug", "hello-world").maybeSingle()
const coverUrl = supatype.storage.publicUrl(post?.cover)
```

The bucket's access rules from the schema decide who may upload, overwrite and delete.

<h2 id="realtime">Realtime</h2>

```ts
const sub = supatype.from("comment").subscribe((change) => {
  console.log(change.eventType, change.new, change.old)
}, { event: "INSERT" })

sub.unsubscribe()
```

Each change reaches only subscribers allowed to read that row. `event` is `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or `*`. For broadcast and presence, use `supatype.realtime.channel(name)`.

<h2 id="functions">Functions</h2>

```ts
const { data: reply, error: fnError } = await supatype.functions.invoke("hello", { body: { name: "Alex" } })
if (fnError) console.error(fnError.code, fnError.message)
console.log(reply)
```

The call goes to `/functions/v1/hello` with the user's token. A JSON response is parsed. Function names and bodies are not typed. `invoke` also takes `method` (default `POST`), `headers` and `idempotent`. Only a `GET` is retried on a transient failure, because a `POST` may already have run. Pass `idempotent: true` when running the function twice is harmless.

```ts
await supatype.functions.invoke("stats", { method: "GET", headers: { "x-region": "eu" } })
```

Inside a function, `ctx.url` is the API's internal address, for calls the function makes. `ctx.publicUrl` is the public address, for links you give to people.

`supatype.rpc(name, params, options)` calls a Postgres function. Its options are `count`, `head`, `schema` for a function outside the default schema, and `idempotent`.

<h2 id="graphql">GraphQL</h2>

```ts
import type { TableRow } from "../supatype/generated/client"

type Post = TableRow<"post">
type Author = TableRow<"author">
type PostPage = {
  postCollection: { edges: { node: Pick<Post, "title" | "body"> & { author: Pick<Author, "name"> } }[] }
}

const { data, error } = await supatype.graphql<PostPage>(`{
  postCollection(first: 10) { edges { node { title body author { name } } } }
}`)
if (error) throw new Error(error.message)
const first = data?.postCollection.edges[0]?.node
console.log(first?.author.name, first?.body.root.children?.[0])
```

The query goes to `/graphql/v1` as the signed-in user, under the same access rules as REST. Pass variables as the second argument, and `{ idempotent: true }` as the third to retry a read on a transient failure.

Rich text, blocks and json fields come back as objects and arrays, not strings. pg_graphql types every json and jsonb column with its `JSON` scalar and sends it as a JSON-encoded string, so the client reads the schema once per role, finds each field of that type in your query, and decodes it. Aliases, named and inline fragments, nested relations and lists all decode. A field the client cannot place stays exactly as returned: one added since the schema was read (it reads the schema again on the next call), a document with more than one operation, or a schema it could not read.

The type argument names the answer's shape and is not checked at runtime. Build it from the generated `TableRow` types so `body` is typed as the rich text document it now is. Variables you send are not encoded: a json argument still takes a string.

Relation fields use your schema's names. The side that holds the key takes the relation field's name, so `author` above. The other side takes its `HasMany` or `HasOne` field's name, so an author's posts are `posts`. A list is still a connection, read through `edges { node }`. REST embeds are named as before.

:::note[Changed in 0.7.0]
GraphQL used to name relations after the tables they join, such as `postCollection` for an author's posts. The next `supatype push` writes the schema's names, and a query that still uses an old name fails with `Unknown field`. A few ambiguous relations keep pg_graphql's own name.
:::

Using another GraphQL client? `readGraphqlSchema` reads the `data` of an introspection answer to `GRAPHQL_SCHEMA_QUERY`, and `decodeGraphqlJsonFields(query, data, schema)` decodes an answer the same way. Read the schema again when it returns `schemaIsStale: true`.

<h2 id="errors">Errors</h2>

Queries, `rpc`, `functions.invoke`, auth and most storage calls return `{ data, error }`. Check `error` before using `data`.

`error` is a plain object with `message` and, when known, `code`, `status`, `details` and `hint`. Do not test it with `instanceof`. When a field validator refused the write, `field` names the column, so you can mark that input.

An insert an access rule refuses returns code `42501`. An update or delete that the rules hide matches no rows and returns no error. `single()` with no row returns `PGRST116`.

:::caution[Network failures]
A network failure on a query, `rpc`, `graphql` or a function call comes back as `error` with a code: `NETWORK_TIMEOUT`, `NETWORK_CONNECTION_REFUSED`, `NETWORK_DNS_FAILURE` or `NETWORK_ERROR`. A read still answered 429 after its last retry has code `RATE_LIMITED`. Most auth and storage calls throw instead, so wrap them in `try` when the network may fail. Three return the failure as `error` like a query: `storage.listBuckets`, `storage.createBucket` and `auth.refreshSession`. `auth.signOut` ignores a network failure and clears the session on this device anyway.
:::

<h2 id="timeouts-and-retries">Timeouts and retries</h2>

Every HTTP request the client makes (tables, `rpc`, `graphql`, `functions`, auth and storage, uploads included) is aborted after `timeout` milliseconds, 30000 by default. Raise it for large uploads on slow links. The realtime socket is not an HTTP request and is not covered.

Only requests that are safe to send twice are retried:

- `GET` and `HEAD` requests: table selects, storage downloads, `auth.getUser()`, and an `rpc` call with `head: true`.
- The two reads storage sends as `POST`: `list` and `createSignedUrl`.
- An `rpc`, `graphql` or `functions.invoke` call you pass `idempotent: true`.

Inserts, updates, upserts, deletes, uploads, sign-in and sign-up, and any `rpc`, `graphql` or function call without `idempotent: true` are sent once: a write that failed in flight may already have been applied, and sending it again could apply it twice. A 429 on one of these comes back as the server's own error.

A retried request is retried up to 3 times, after 200 ms, 1 s and 3 s, on a dropped connection or a 5xx. A 429 waits for its `Retry-After` (5 seconds when the header is absent). A timeout and a 4xx are never retried. `retry: false` turns retries off for every request.

```ts
const { data, error } = await supatype.rpc(
  "search_posts",
  { query: "supatype" },
  { idempotent: true }, // the function only reads, so a retry is harmless
)
```
